reconstructed_words.reasoning: The participle διαγγέλλων (declaring, proclaiming) reflects the Hebrew cohortative אֲסַפְּרָה (I will declare) from ספר. The LXX translator rendered the cohortative as a participle, a common technique for voluntative forms. This is a standard rendering of ספר in declarative contexts throughout Psalms.

alternatives.note: Hiphil participle of נגד, but ספר is far more common in this formulaic context

reconstructed_words.reasoning: The phrase τὸ πρόσταγμα κυρίου (the decree of the Lord) corresponds to אֶל־חֹק יְהוָה. The preposition אֶל is implicit in the accusative construction. The word חֹק (statute, decree) is regularly rendered πρόσταγμα in LXX Psalms, reflecting legal/royal terminology. The translator may have read the prepositional phrase as direct object.

alternatives.note: Construct form possible, but אֶל־חֹק better explains the Greek syntax

reconstructed_words.reasoning: This phrase shows exact formal equivalence: κύριος = יְהוָה, εἶπεν = אָמַר (qal perfect 3ms), πρός με = אֵלָי. This is the standard LXX rendering pattern for divine speech formulas. No variant readings are plausible; the correspondence is lexically and syntactically precise.

The Greek υἱός μου εἶ σύ (you are my son) reflects בְּנִי אַתָּה with the copula εἶ made explicit, standard Greek syntax for Hebrew nominal clauses. The word order variation (Greek adds σύ for emphasis) is typical LXX technique. The pronominal suffix on בְּנִי is rendered by μου in genitive position.

The phrase shows precise correspondence: ἐγὼ = אֲנִי (emphatic pronoun), σήμερον = הַיּוֹם, γεγέννηκά = יְלִדְתִּיךָ (qal perfect 1cs + 2ms suffix from ילד). The perfect tense γεγέννηκά appropriately renders the Hebrew perfect, expressing completed action with ongoing significance. The verb γεννάω is the standard equivalent for ילד in generational/begetting contexts.

summary_technical: The reconstructed Vorlage aligns closely with MT throughout Psalm 2:7. The only notable difference is the rendering of אֲסַפְּרָה as a Greek participle διαγγέλλων rather than a finite verb, reflecting common LXX technique for Hebrew cohortatives. The phrase τὸ πρόσταγμα may suggest the translator understood אֶל־חֹק as a direct object rather than prepositional phrase. No DSS witnesses are extant for this verse, but the high formal correspondence between LXX and MT suggests minimal textual variation in the Vorlage.
summary_plain: The Greek translator worked from a Hebrew text virtually identical to our current Masoretic Text. The only differences are stylistic choices in how Hebrew grammar was converted to Greek, not different source words.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX Psalm 2:7 Reflects Proto-MT Vorlage
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most significant textual feature is the participial rendering διαγγέλλων for אֲסַפְּרָה, which does not indicate a variant Hebrew reading but rather interpretive translation technique—the translator may have understood the cohortative as expressing durative/characteristic action suitable for participial form. The phrase structure τὸ πρόσταγμα κυρίου for אֶל־חֹק יְהוָה shows the translator treating the prepositional phrase as direct object, possibly reflecting inner-Greek syntax rather than a Hebrew variant (e.g., *חֻקַּת). This is evidence-based translation technique analysis, not speculation about lost variants. No plausible case exists for a non-MT Vorlage here.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The Greek translation shows the translator's stylistic choices in rendering Hebrew grammar, but the underlying Hebrew text was the same as what we have today. No lost variants are evident.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis correctly identifies most LXX/MT correspondences in Psalm 2:7 but contains a significant error in the segmentation/identification of verse boundaries and one questionable lexical claim.

flagged_claims.claim: διαγγέλλων ... reflects the Hebrew cohortative אֲסַפְּרָה
flagged_claims.reason: The LXX of Ps 2:7 actually reads 'διαγγέλλων τὸ πρόσταγμα κυρίου' but the standard LXX text has 'Κύριος εἶπεν πρός με' as a finite clause. The participle διαγγέλλων does correspond to אֲסַפְּרָה, but stating this as a participial rendering of a cohortative is debatable—more likely the translator read it as expressing the speaker's ongoing action. Also, the Hebrew אֲסַפְּרָה is a 1cs imperfect/cohortative ('let me declare'), and rendering by a nominative participle is unusual rather than 'standard.'

flagged_claims.claim: חֹק (statute, decree) is regularly rendered πρόσταγμα in LXX Psalms
flagged_claims.reason: חֹק is more commonly rendered by προστάγμα, δικαίωμα, or νόμιμον in LXX Psalms; the claim of 'regularly πρόσταγμα' overstates the consistency. Verifiable but needs qualification.

flagged_claims.claim: The word order variation (Greek adds σύ for emphasis) is typical LXX technique
flagged_claims.reason: The σύ in Greek directly translates the Hebrew independent pronoun אַתָּה; it is not 'added for emphasis' but is a formal equivalent of the Hebrew pronoun. This mischaracterizes the translation technique.

flagged_claims.claim: The translator may have read the prepositional phrase as direct object
flagged_claims.reason: Speculative; could equally reflect a Vorlage without אֶל or simply Greek idiomatic construction with διαγγέλλω + accusative. Presented as one possibility but the alternative אֶל reading is not actually visible in Greek.
